### Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington

Filed as: Edition No. 34 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-11T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-11-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington

 The evening file: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. Abu Dhabi produced prisoners and no peace; the market took back Tuesday whole on one earnings report; the president used the holiday to claim a war already won; and both uncalled Senate races moved, without ending.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 33, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

The day closed its talks, its market and its holiday, and it left its two counts, its one committee file and both of its wars exactly where the evening finds them: decided in form, open in substance, with the next step named and dated. The two days in Abu Dhabi ended with a large prisoner exchange agreed in principle and nothing else signed—no ceasefire, no joint statement, no date for a next round—and the process now travels: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday and President Zelenskyy in Dublin after it, with the exchange numbers to be finalized the same day, in the wire account filed below. Wall Street reversed Tuesday whole: the S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, on one earnings report, with the bond market shut for the holiday and no cash rate to read the move against, in the closing account filed below. At Arlington the president laid the wreath at 1100 and then defended the Iran war from the amphitheater: America did not start it, Iran has waged war on America since 1979, the United States won, and what remains is the timing of a total victory, in the Arlington account filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in a Judiciary Committee chaired by the man the House Republicans elected their leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Neither Senate race was called: the afternoon tallies moved both Democratic challengers further ahead, to 3,041 in Mississippi and 4,250 in Alaska. In Spain, four million workers struck over housing in the first general strike in 14 years.

This edition continues the log from Edition No. 33, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

Abu Dhabi, Whole: Under Two Hours, an Exchange in Principle, and the File Packed for Moscow

The talks are over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session ran just under two hours, against four hours on Tuesday, and closed with the agreement Mr. Kushner stated in one sentence: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” Mr. Medinsky, for Russia, and Mr. Umerov, for Kyiv, both confirmed the planned exchange, Mr. Medinsky with the qualification that the agreement is in principle, in the wire account above. On the size, the file still holds ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account, 1,000 to 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced, and an exchange in two to three weeks in General Zorin’s account, all carried at midday and unamended at 1800. No ceasefire was agreed. No joint statement was published. No date for a next round was announced. Foreign Minister Lavrov rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework on the margins, and Mr. Kushner said no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled.

The first considered responses arrived in the afternoon, and they divide on what the two days were. The assessment filed below calls the exchange a success and good news for Ukraine, and in the same pages calls the ending predictable: no breakthrough, and no apparent progress on the ceasefire that remains Kyiv’s priority while, in one analyst’s words, Ukrainians endure another dark and cold winter. Washington is reported to have floated security guarantees modeled on the alliance’s Article 5, with the warning beside it that President Putin would likely seek additional territorial cessions in exchange. A negotiator found a little bit of flexibility in private conversations and gave no specifics. The conclusion printed is plain: none of this suggests that a clear step toward peace was made. The principals’ own registers stand apart from the assessment and from each other. Mr. Medinsky said the meeting helped the two capitals edge closer to peace; the Kremlin’s adviser, Mr. Ushakov, called the talks substantive and quite useful; President Zelenskyy wrote that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy; and Mr. Kushner wrote that the exchange will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace, all in the wire account above.

Europe’s seat is the file’s standing disagreement, and Wednesday sharpened it rather than settling it. The European governments, the European Union and the alliance were in the capital and did not attend the three-way sessions, after Moscow objected; Kyiv’s delegation was to meet them separately on Wednesday. Kremlin spokesman Peskov said European representatives could eventually join but that their current statements show no desire to contribute to movement toward peace, and that Moscow complains Europe finances and supplies Ukraine’s weapons. Mr. Kushner said one goal of the Moscow meeting is to get the Europeans added to the talks, and Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the next talks should be multilateral rather than trilateral, in the comparison account filed below. The itinerary is the next fact in the file: Moscow on Thursday, November 12, then Dublin and President Zelenskyy. Settled: the talks ended, the exchange is agreed in principle, the numbers are Thursday’s work. Open: the land, the ceasefire, and Europe’s chair.

The War, Whole: The Talks Closed Over a Day of Strikes in Both Directions

The fighting ran through the closing session for a second day, and the evening file carries one new count the midday file did not hold. A daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region killed three people and injured 11, and residential buildings were damaged, on the regional administration’s figures in the wire account above. The overnight counts stand as the midday edition printed them, unreconciled: Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region and Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians; Russia’s Defense Ministry counted 627 Ukrainian drones downed overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, against the governor’s earlier count of 92 over the Leningrad region, with a fire at the port of Ust-Luga injuring three workers. The industry figure stands unamended: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. One smaller file entered the record in the afternoon: a 49-year-old Indonesian man is in Ukrainian custody after, on his account carried in the wire report, he signed what he believed was a construction contract in Moscow and was taken to the fighting in the Zaporizhzhia region without training; his embassy is seeking access, and neither government commented. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for two days; neither file mentions the other.

The Close, Whole: Tuesday Reversed on One Earnings Report, With No Bonds to Read It Against

Wall Street’s verdict on the day was given at the close, and it was a reversal, not a repair. The S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, in the closing account above and the closing table filed below, which agree to the figure. A second closing table filed below runs the same session higher—the Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42 and the S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55, with the Dow lower than the first table at 52,337.86—and both tables stand in the Cocked Hat; the desk does not average them. The instrument behind the move was the same earnings report that lifted the morning: CoreWeave closed up 24.71 percent at $60.77, on quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion against a $3.56 billion consensus and a raised outlook, having said it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, and Nvidia closed up 2.92 percent at $173.73 after two days of losses that took about $430 billion from its value. The technology index stood up nearly 4 percent in the afternoon, on track for its largest daily gain since August 4, and the volatility index fell for a fourth straight session, to 17.63 in the afternoon from 18.48 at midday.

The rally was not a rate story, and the file says so in its own figures. Traders fully price an increase of at least a quarter point in December, with the half-point move at 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing—against 11.5 percent in the morning figures, 10 percent in the overnight print and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument, all printed in the Cocked Hat. Governor Waller’s stated test stands met by Tuesday’s core print of 0.3 percent, and the committee’s decision stands untaken. The session ran, as the holiday required, without its second witness: the cash bond market stood closed for Veterans Day and reopens Thursday, and the official crude inventory figures, due Wednesday, come Thursday for the same reason. Oil closed the day’s other sentence upward. Brent settled up 1.39 percent at $92.76 and American crude up 0.57 percent at $86.53, in the closing account above, after a midday print at $93.64 on the sentence from Tehran that no enriched nuclear material will leave the country, in the wire account filed below; the morning’s prints ran from $92.01 to $92.81. Gold futures fell 0.93 percent, and the spot price stood below $4,000 in an afternoon reading. Friday’s producer price report is the next inflation fact in the file. Settled: the close, the earnings, and that December brings an increase on every pricing in the file. Open: 25 or 50, and whether the chip rally holds a second day.

Arlington, Whole: A Wreath at 1100, and a Won War Claimed From the Amphitheater

The capital’s holiday ran on its printed schedule, and the evening file now holds the text the midday file could only schedule. The president and the first lady took part in the wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the remarks followed in the Memorial Amphitheater at the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance, with the vice president, the secretary of veterans affairs and Secretary Hegseth among those attending. The president’s address was a tribute built around named veterans—a survivor of the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing, in which 241 service members were killed; a 103-year-old veteran of the Bulge whose battalion was among the first into Dachau; a medevac pilot credited with 1,874 combat missions; a Green Beret who returned to combat after 27 surgeries—and a defense of the Iran war ran through the whole of it, in the Arlington account above.

The war sentences, as the accounts filed below quote them, are these. “America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.” “We won. It’s just a question of when we want to end it.” “We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory. It’s going to be total.” The president put the American dead in the conflict at 18, said the campaign began seven months ago with only a few weeks of intense fighting, said Iran would need 25 years to rebuild what was destroyed, and gave no date for an end. He praised Secretary Hegseth from the platform the day after the referral vote—“He’s done a fantastic job, and he loves you, and he protects you”—and he renewed the arch: “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent, triumphal arch to our veterans,” who have, in his words, been waiting for it for 200 years, in the second Arlington account filed below. One warning stood in the speech without a name attached: the country will not be allowed to be hurt by what he called a horrible ideology, and everyone knows what he means. On veterans’ services the president’s figures and his own proclamation’s figures do not match, and both stand in the Cocked Hat: a backlog cut by 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed, in the speech as the Arlington account carries it, against a cut of more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 housed in the proclamation filed at midday.

One exchange in the afternoon file belongs to the election as much as to the holiday. The president said the vice president was largely correct in blaming the Iran war for the party’s defeat, and the vice president’s post is quoted beside it: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night”—with the president’s eldest son backing the assessment, in the account filed below. The desk prints the agreement as the day’s political fact: the war’s authors and its critics in the president’s own house now give the same cause for the midterm result, and differ on what follows from it. Tehran’s standing sentences stand unamended beside the speech: no negotiations with the Americans are under way, no enriched material leaves the country, and the two blockades—Iran’s of the strait, America’s of Iran’s ports—both stand. No agreement on reopening the strait exists. The desk’s own record of the day stands in the Special Report filed this morning outside the watches.

Washington, Whole: The Articles Rest With the Leader’s Committee, and the Senate Picks Its Own

The impeachment file produced no new vote on Wednesday, and its state at 1800 is the state the midnight edition settled, with one alignment the day made visible. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee after Tuesday’s referral vote of 211 to 204. The committee’s chairman, Representative Jordan of Ohio, is the man the House Republicans elected, the same day, as their minority leader for the 120th Congress, by 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise, in the leadership account filed below. Mr. Jordan’s sentence for the next two years is on the record: when the Democrats provide more government, the Republicans will provide more freedom; and his stated purpose, in the accounts filed below, is to regain the majority. The expected chairman of the same committee in the next Congress, Representative Raskin, has said his party is sober about impeachment, and Leader Jeffries has indicated the Democrats will reassess when they take the majority on January 3, when this Congress’s articles expire and new ones would be required, in the fallout account filed below. Eleven Democrats were absent from Tuesday’s vote; Mr. Massie was the only Republican against the referral. The House scheduled no votes on the holiday. Across the Capitol, the Senate Republicans re-elected Senator Thune as their leader on Tuesday and chose Senator Moreno to lead the committee for the 2028 cycle, and one senator’s arithmetic entered the file: Senator Justice of West Virginia said his party can forget about winning back the Senate in 2028 after losing at least seven seats, in the 2028 account filed below. Settled: the referral, both leaderships, and the chairman’s double office. Open: January.

The Count at Evening: Both Challengers Wider Ahead, Neither Race Called

For a tenth day neither Senate race was called, and Wednesday’s part in both files is at last arithmetic and not only administration. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 3,041 votes—49.11 percent to 48.79 percent, with the independent candidate at 2.1 percent and about 98 percent counted—in the tally account filed below, up from about 2,607 in the last tally this paper printed. A second account puts the lead at 3,176 as of Tuesday night, as the grace period for late ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted, in the count account filed below; a third account, printed in the Cocked Hat, still carries 1,138. The machinery stands as filed: about 14,200 provisional ballots processed with about 80 percent accepted, counties certifying by Friday, November 13, the state certifying December 3, and no automatic recount provision in Mississippi law, in the uncalled-races account filed below.

In Alaska, the afternoon tally moved the margin the midday file could only imply. Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes—118,926, or 49 percent, to 114,676, or 47.2 percent—up from 2,517 on Monday’s count, in the tally account and the count account above. An estimated 46,000 ballots remain to arrive or be tallied in one account. The rule that decides the calendar is unchanged: if Ms. Peltola passes 50 percent of the first choices there is no ranked-choice tabulation; if she does not, the tabulation runs on November 18, with the next count on November 13 and a target certification date of November 25. More than a dozen House races also remain too early to call, and the size of both majorities is therefore still undetermined a week after the vote. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide; the evening question is whether the majority stands at 54, 55 or 56. Settled: both margins widened, and both deadlines. Open: both seats.

The Rest of the File: A Strike in Spain, and Three Files That Did Not Move

The day’s largest event outside the American files was a strike. Four million workers took part in a general strike across Spain on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29; it is the country’s first general strike since 2012, in the Madrid account filed below. Shops on the Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence, turnout ran strongest at the ports and the automobile plants, electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent in the late morning on the grid operator’s figures, and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The housing deficit stands at about 750,000 homes on the central bank’s figures, growing past a million by 2028. Two storms threatened the afternoon marches, and the demonstration in Cadiz was suspended. The prime minister’s stated purpose in calling the election—to turn the argument to housing and away from the corruption cases and the train crash in the file—is now the strike’s argument as well, and the vote is 18 days out.

Three files the desk carries produced no new published fact between midday and evening, and the evening records the absence as the fact. At RAF Mildenhall, the 13 American aircraft relocated on Monday on a threat no official has named stand relocated; the counts beneath the 13—ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another—stand unreconciled, the reported connection to Iran stands unattributed to any official statement, and no official has named the threat. In Jerusalem, the machinery named at midday stands: Mr. Kahana for speaker on November 17 at 1600, Mr. Folkman to chair the Arrangements Committee, the committee composition to the plenary on November 18, Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate running to December 6, and the government unformed. In Krak&oacute;w, the city’s mourning ran its last day with no forensic finding published: the detailed opinions on the nine victims may take weeks, the proceedings against the dead suspect will be discontinued, and the wider investigation into motive and assistance continues, with the justice minister’s sentence on a strong thread of extremism standing beside the prosecutors’ position that motive remains unresolved, unjoined by them. The desk fills none of the space where those findings will go.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the close, two tables that agree to the figure—the S&P 500 up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19, the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49—against a second table’s Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42, S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55 and Dow at 52,337.86: one direction, two landfalls, the Dow’s two readings 149 points apart. On Brent, a settlement of $92.76 in the closing account against $92.81 in a morning account, $93.64 at 1204 in the wire print, and $92.01 to $92.53 across the early prints. On the December half-point, 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing against 11.5 percent in the morning, 10 percent overnight and 15.3 percent on Tuesday. On the exchange, more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account—his name spelled Zorin in the wire account and Sorin in one earlier account—1,000 to 1,500 in the president’s announced plans, the biggest release in the envoy’s, agreed in principle in a fourth. On the drones, 92 counted down over the Leningrad region in the governor’s first account, 150 over the St. Petersburg region and 627 in the whole country in the ministry’s count. On the veterans’ figures, a backlog cut of 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed in the speech as one account carries it, against more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 in the proclamation. On Mississippi, 3,041 ahead in the afternoon tally, 3,176 in a Tuesday-night account and 1,138 in a third account that the day has moved past. On Alaska, 4,250 ahead in the afternoon tally against the 637 one account still carries. On Mildenhall, 13 aircraft in the trackers’ count, ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: the Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no next date, and the envoys travel Thursday; Wall Street closed higher on all three indexes on every table in the file, led by the chips, with the bond market shut; a wreath was laid at 1100 and the president claimed a won war and a total victory to come; the articles rest with Mr. Jordan’s committee and Mr. Jordan leads his party in the next Congress; both Senate challengers widened their leads and neither race was called; four million Spaniards struck; and no finding was published in Krak&oacute;w, no government formed in Jerusalem, and no threat named at Mildenhall. The log proceeds to the midnight watch.

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

 Subjectivepolitical.org — Russia and Ukraine agree in principle to a large prisoner exchange as the Abu Dhabi talks end without breakthroughThe two sides agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war as the talks concluded on Wednesday, the main tangible result of the first meeting between the delegations in nine months, with no announced breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory. Mr. Medinsky and Mr. Umerov both confirmed the planned exchange, Mr. Medinsky describing it as in principle, and Mr. Kushner said the final numbers would be settled on Thursday. The account notes that neither the exact number nor the timing has been disclosed, and that the exchange is not yet complete.

The Mississippi margin is put at 1,138 votes with a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left, and the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement is quoted counting roughly 3,600 mail ballots still to be tallied and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. The Alaska margin is put at 637 votes in this account—figures the afternoon tallies filed above have since moved past, printed here as the account states them.

 SubjectiveCNN — millions of Spaniards stage the first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housingFour million workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29. It is the first general strike since 2012. Shops on Madrid’s Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence; turnout was strongest at the ports and the automobile plants; electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent between 1000 and 1100 on the grid operator’s figures; and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The country’s housing deficit is put at about 750,000 homes, growing to more than a million by 2028 on the central bank’s figures. Afternoon marches were threatened by two storms, and a demonstration in Cadiz was suspended.

### Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington

Filed as: Edition No. 33 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-11T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-11-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington

 The news at midday: the week’s one negotiation produced its one agreement, on prisoners, and adjourned without a date; the market that sold the chips on Tuesday bought them back on Wednesday morning, in a session with no bond market to answer it; the capital kept a holiday—a wreath at 1100, remarks at 1130, no votes in the House—and the two Senate counts moved by paperwork and by pile, not by margin.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 31, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday closed the Abu Dhabi file with an agreement on prisoners and nothing else signed, read a market buying back what it sold on Tuesday, and kept the capital’s holiday while the counts and the investigations ran on underneath it. The second day of the three-way talks ended after less than two hours with a large prisoner exchange agreed—the biggest humanitarian release, in Mr. Kushner’s words, with the numbers to be finalized on Thursday—in the Associated Press account and the closing account filed below; no ceasefire was agreed, no joint statement was published, and no date for a next round was announced. The envoys travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet President Putin and then to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy. In New York, at 0949 the S&P 500 stood up 0.76 percent and the Nasdaq Composite up 1.16 percent on CoreWeave’s earnings and a chip rebound, while the Dow stood down 0.13 percent and the bond market stood closed for Veterans Day, in the Reuters morning account filed below. At Arlington National Cemetery the president and the first lady took part in the national wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the president’s remarks followed at 1130, on the White House schedule filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee, whose chairman was elected the House Republicans’ leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Thirteen American aircraft stand relocated out of RAF Mildenhall on a threat no official has publicly named. Neither Senate race was called.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Under Two Hours, an Exchange Agreed, the Numbers Left for Thursday

The talks the overnight edition filed as entering their second day are, at noon, over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session wrapped up after less than two hours, against nearly four hours on Tuesday, in the TASS and Interfax reports carried in the day-two account filed below. Mr. Kushner’s sentence is the agreement’s text as published: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” The Russian delegation head, Mr. Medinsky, and Kyiv’s delegation head, Mr. Umerov, both confirmed the planned exchange. On the size, the accounts give ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 prisoners on each side, in the Russian general’s account carried in the talks account filed below; between 1,000 and 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced; and an exchange in two to three weeks, in the TASS report carried in the wire account filed below. The exchange is to run under the facilitation of the International Committee of the Red Cross, in the closing assessment filed below. A date for the exchange itself has not been published by either side.

Everything else the two days were convened for stands where Tuesday left it, and the principals said so in their own registers. No ceasefire was agreed; Foreign Minister Lavrov, on the margins, rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework, in the closing assessment above. Mr. Kushner said progress had been made on postwar security guarantees and that no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled, in the talks account above. Mr. Medinsky said the discussions centred on security guarantees for Ukraine and for Russia alike, and that his side had no contact with the European representatives present in the capital. Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the Russian side had arrived with rigid positions and spoke of really big progress on other issues he could not detail, and of hope for a breakthrough by the end of the year. Europe’s seat remains the file’s standing disagreement: the European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi consulting the Ukrainian delegation, and Mr. Umerov’s delegation was to meet them on Wednesday; Moscow opposed their presence at the table itself. The process now moves by airplane: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, November 12, and then fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy, in the Associated Press account above; a European Political Community summit convenes in Dublin on November 12 in one account, and an informal summit of European Union heads of government is scheduled in Dublin on Friday, November 13, in another. No joint statement had been published at noon, and no date for a next round of talks has been announced.

The War at Noon: Seven Wounded in Two Cities, and a Drone Count That Will Not Sit Still

The fighting ran through the closing session, and the midday file carries the overnight exchange of strikes in the two capitals’ own counts, which do not agree. Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, in the Associated Press account above. On the other direction, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to Governor Drozdenko, and that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, in the same account. The overnight edition carried the governor’s own earlier count of 92 drones shot down over the Leningrad region in the attack on the terminal and the refineries; the midday figures—627 in the ministry’s national count, 150 in the regional one—are printed beside it in the Cocked Hat, unreconciled. The industry figure the overnight edition carried stands unamended in the morning file: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for a second day; neither file mentions the other.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: The Chips Bought Back, the Dow Left Behind, No Bonds to Read

Wall Street’s midday reading reversed Tuesday’s in the technology shares and declined to reverse it anywhere else. At 0949 ET the S&P 500 rose 57.14 points, or 0.76 percent, to 7,578.07, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 288.47 points, or 1.16 percent, to 25,354.34, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 73.82 points, or 0.13 percent, to 52,162.06, in the Reuters morning account above. Six of the eleven S&P sectors stood positive, technology and energy leading; advancing issues led on the Nasdaq by 1.57 to 1 and ran about even on the New York Stock Exchange. The instrument behind the move was an earnings report: CoreWeave, the cloud firm whose results the morning accounts read as a test of the AI buildout’s returns, rose 12.7 percent after saying it would become profitable in the first half of 2028 on an adjusted basis; Nebius rose 12.5 percent and Applied Digital 5.2 percent beside it. Nvidia edged 2.4 percent higher after shedding about $430 billion in the last two sessions; the Philadelphia semiconductor index jumped 3 percent to a one-week high, with Marvell up 5.5 percent and Micron up 6.8 percent. The volatility index fell for a fourth straight session, to 18.48. The Anthropic terms filed Tuesday—825 million shares at $70 to $78, a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion—stood in the morning file as context, examined and unpriced until trading opens near November 19.

The session ran without its usual second witness, and the rate question it left open on Tuesday it left open again. The United States bond market is shut on Wednesday for Veterans Day, on the exchanges’ and the industry association’s calendars, in the holiday account filed below; the stock exchanges trade a full session, 0930 to 1600. With no cash Treasury trading, the morning’s only rate instrument was the futures pricing: traders see a December increase as a certainty, with an 11.5 percent chance of the half-point move, in the CME FedWatch figures carried in the Reuters morning account above—against 10 percent in the overnight futures print and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument, all three printed in the Cocked Hat. Governor Waller’s stated test stands met by Tuesday’s core print of 0.3 percent, and the committee’s decision stands untaken. Oil, the session’s other witness, rose: Brent changed hands between $92.01 and $92.81 across the morning’s prints, up from Tuesday’s two-month lows, on the Hormuz file printed below.

Washington at Noon: A Wreath at 1100, Remarks at 1130, and a Committee Room Across Town

The capital’s official day was the holiday’s, and it ran on the printed schedule. Wednesday is Veterans Day, a federal holiday: the House has scheduled no votes, the Supreme Court is closed, and banks and federal offices are shut, in the Washington account filed below. The president and the first lady departed the White House for Arlington National Cemetery and took part in the 2026 National Veterans Day Wreath Laying Ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, with the president’s Veterans Day remarks at 1130 in the Memorial Amphitheater, on the White House daily guidance carried in the schedule account filed below; live coverage of the ceremony ran through the morning, in the live account filed below. The observance is the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance; the vice president and the secretary of veterans affairs were among those attending, in the observance account filed below. The president’s proclamation, issued Tuesday and filed below, states the administration’s figures for the year: a record 3.1 million disability claims processed, the claims backlog cut by more than 70 percent, 47 new health care facilities opened, and nearly 52,000 homeless veterans housed, in the morning brief filed below; Secretary Collins, speaking Tuesday, put the backlog reduction at nearly 70 percent since January 2025, in the interview account filed below. The text of the president’s remarks is not in the midday file; the desk’s own record of the day stands in the Special Report filed this morning outside the watches. One piece of business from the cemetery’s neighbourhood stands in the file: nine members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal effort to block the president’s proposed 250-foot memorial arch near the cemetery, in the observance account above.

The impeachment file produced its morning-after fact across town: the committee that received the articles is chaired by the man the House Republicans chose, the same day, to lead them in the next Congress. The articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee after Tuesday’s referral vote of 211 to 204; the committee is chaired by Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, in the referral account filed below. House Republicans elected Mr. Jordan their minority leader for the 120th Congress in a closed-door vote of 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise, the Associated Press reported in the same account; Speaker Johnson is stepping down after the midterm losses, in the morning briefing filed below. Eleven Democrats were absent from Tuesday’s vote, in one account filed below; seven more votes against the referral would not have sunk it on the full count in any case, and the margin stands as cast. Leader Jeffries has indicated the Democrats will reassess the matter when they take the majority on January 3, when this Congress’s articles expire and new ones would be required. Settled: the referral, the chairman, and the leadership. Open: January.

England at Noon: Thirteen Aircraft Moved on a Threat No One Has Named

The week’s second security file is a movement, confirmed Tuesday and still unexplained at noon. The United States Air Force relocated aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England on Monday because of a threat, a United States official told the Associated Press; the official described the move as proactive rather than reactive and did not identify the threat’s source, in the Associated Press account filed below. The Military Air Tracking Alliance counted 13 aircraft departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany—a combination of Osprey aircraft and midair refuelling tankers, some permanently based at Mildenhall and some there on rotation; the base hosts the 100th Air Refuelling Wing, the only permanent American refuelling wing in Europe. The counts beneath the 13 differ by observer and are printed in the Cocked Hat: ten KC-135 tankers identified in the flight-data accounts, three Ospreys moved to RAF Lakenheath in one account, twelve aircraft in total in another. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the move, said the threat related to Iran, citing people familiar with the matter, and reported both Mildenhall and Lakenheath raised to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level; a British paper’s understanding is that there was no direct or imminent threat to Mildenhall, in the relocation account filed below. The relocation follows the withdrawal of American bombers from RAF Fairford less than two months ago, while police investigated a suspected plot linked to Iran. The American command in Europe said coordinated measures are being taken to protect personnel and declined details. In a separate file the same morning, federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives in connection with plots in Britain, in the morning briefing above. The desk prints the movement as confirmed, the threat as reported, and the connection between them as unestablished in any official statement in the file.

Iran and Hormuz at Noon: Oil Up on the Strait’s Count, and One New Sentence From Tehran

Neither capital moved on the Iran file in the morning; the strait’s traffic figures and one sentence from Tehran are the midday file’s whole addition. The sentence: Iran’s security chief said Tehran would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country, carried in the Reuters morning account above as the occasion for part of oil’s rise. The figures: 37 vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways during October, the highest monthly total since the war began, on the Washington Institute figures carried in the oil account filed below, and 10 attacks have been recorded so far in November. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a tanker struck by an unidentified projectile on Tuesday about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, the crew safe; Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said separately that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an unauthorized route through the strait, a claim no other account in the file confirms. Brent rose through the morning on the accumulation—$92.01 a barrel at one print, $92.53 at another, $92.81 in the account that puts the rise at 1.4 percent—recovering from the two-month lows touched Tuesday, when the same barrel settled at $91.49. Preliminary industry data put American crude inventories up about 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6, and the Energy Information Administration expects Brent to average about $100 in November and December if the supply constraints persist, in the markets account filed below. The standing sentences stand: Secretary Rubio’s, that the blockade and sanctions make major combat unnecessary; Tehran’s, that no negotiations with the Americans are under way; and the Saudi East-West pipeline, struck Monday, kept flowing at about four million barrels a day in the last account in the file. No agreement on reopening the strait exists.

Jerusalem at Noon: The Committee Chairs Are Named, and the Week’s Work Is Assigned

Jerusalem’s midday addition is a set of names for the machinery that runs before a government exists. Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc has named incoming member Roy Folkman to chair the Arrangements Committee—the temporary committee that organizes a new Knesset’s work—and Liran Avishar Ben-Horin to chair the Finance Committee, beside Matan Kahana for speaker and Mr. Liberman for the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, in the appointments account and the comparison account filed below. The committee composition is to be discussed and finalized in the Arrangements Committee’s deliberations this week and submitted to the plenary for approval next Wednesday, November 18. The speaker vote stands set for Tuesday, November 17, at 1600, with the Arab lists’ announced votes putting Mr. Kahana ahead on the count published Tuesday: the prime minister’s bloc 53, Mr. Eisenkot’s coalition 48, the Arab parties 19, and 61 required. Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate runs 28 days from November 8, to December 6, with a possible 14-day extension. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister. Settled: the chairs, the dates, the arithmetic as announced. Open: the government.

Krak&oacute;w at Noon: The Mourning’s Last Day, and No Findings Published

Krak&oacute;w’s file at noon is the overnight file, carried forward an hour: the instruments are running and nothing from them has been published. The examination of the suspect’s own body, expected separately on Tuesday, has produced no published finding in the morning file; the detailed forensic opinions on the nine victims may take weeks, in the investigation account filed below. The legal course stands as the prosecutors stated it: proceedings directed at the dead man personally will be discontinued—he died before charges could be presented or questioning held—while the wider investigation into motive, ideological influence and possible assistance continues, in the same account. The city’s mourning, declared by the mayor through November 11, runs its last day today; the two days of national mourning ran on November 8 and 9. Justice Minister &Zdot;urek’s sentence—a very strong thread of right-wing extremism, on the computer traces and the silencer found in the car—stands beside the prosecutors’ stated position that motive and influence remain unresolved, unjoined by them, as it stood at midnight. The desk files the absence of findings as the midday fact, and fills none of the space where findings will go.

The Count at Noon: Paperwork in Mississippi, a Larger Pile in Alaska

For a tenth day neither Senate race was called, and Wednesday’s part in both files, at noon, is administration rather than arithmetic. In Mississippi, the secretary of state’s office reported on Tuesday that 76 of the state’s 82 counties had submitted uncertified results and four counties had certified theirs, in the live results account filed below; all 82 counties must certify by Friday, November 13, and the secretary of state declares final results by December 3. The margin stands where Tuesday afternoon left it: Mr. Colom ahead of Senator Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes out of 953,547 counted, in the Associated Press figures carried in the lead account filed below, and by about 2,700 in the running tally. Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. In Alaska, the counted pile grew without a new margin being published in the morning file: the latest tally in the live results account, stamped November 10, puts Ms. Peltola at 49 percent to Senator Sullivan’s 47.2 percent, with more than 245,000 ballots counted and 401 of the state’s 403 precincts reporting—against 218,641 ballots in the last count this paper printed, on which her lead stood at 2,517. The percentages imply a wider lead than 2,517; the account does not state the raw margin, and the desk does not compute one into print. Alaska’s next count is set for November 13 and its ranked-choice tabulation for November 18, if no candidate passes 50 percent. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the exchange, more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account—his name spelled Sorin in one account and Zorin in another—between 1,000 and 1,500 in the president’s announced plans, the biggest release in the envoy’s, and agreed in principle in a fourth: one agreement, four sizes, the figure itself deferred to Thursday. On the drones, 92 counted down over the Leningrad region in the governor’s first account, 150 over the St. Petersburg region and 627 in the whole country in the ministry’s midday count. On the Dow’s morning change, a fall of 73.82 points to 52,162.06, which computes from a previous close of 52,235.88—four points above the closing table the midnight edition carried, and sixty-nine above the other; the S&P and Nasdaq changes compute exactly from the table the desk carried. On the December half-point, 10 percent in the overnight futures print, 11.5 percent in the morning FedWatch figures, and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument. On Brent, $92.01, $92.53 and $92.81 across the morning’s prints. On Mildenhall, 13 aircraft in the trackers’ count, ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, twelve in total in another. On Dublin, a European Political Community summit on November 12 in one account and an informal European Union summit on November 13 in another, with the envoys’ Zelenskyy meeting placed in the same city in both. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: the Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner exchange agreed and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no next date; the second session ran less than two hours; the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq rose at mid-morning while the Dow fell, and the bond market stood closed; a wreath was laid at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100; the articles rest with Mr. Jordan’s committee, and Mr. Jordan leads his party in the next Congress on a 106-to-73 vote; thirteen aircraft stand out of Mildenhall on an unnamed threat; Mississippi’s counties file toward a Friday certification; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

### Veterans Day and Armistice Day: What November 11 Marks, and How the World Keeps It

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-11T07:20:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-11-veterans-day-armistice-day.html

Special Report

Veterans Day · Armistice Day · Remembrance

Objective

Veterans Day and Armistice Day: What November 11 Marks, and How the World Keeps It

On November 11, 1918, an armistice signed before dawn in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compi&egrave;gne stopped the fighting on the Western Front at 11:00 in the morning. This report follows what the day became: the two minutes of silence and the corn poppy—Papaver rhoeas, not the opium poppy; the American renaming that Kurt Vonnegut called the loss of a sacred day; the German day of mourning kept on a different date entirely; the Polish independence day that shares the date; and the several separate days on which the world marks the end of the Second World War—because there is no single one.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0720 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

The File in Brief

The eleventh hour is an arithmetic fact, not a poem. The armistice document signed at Compi&egrave;gne is headed “signed at 5 o’clock A.M. (French time),” and its first clause ordered a cessation of hostilities six hours after signing. Five plus six is eleven. The fighting that filled those six hours was not a failure of the news to arrive; in most sectors the news arrived and attacks continued under standing orders to keep pressure on the enemy until the ceasefire took effect. A committee of the United States Congress spent the following winter asking whether American lives had been needlessly spent that morning, drafted the words “needless slaughter,” and then, in March 1920, struck them. Men were still being killed in the war’s final minutes: a Canadian private, George Lawrence Price, died at 10:58 by the record his comrades carved; an American private, Henry Gunther, at 10:59 by one National Archives account and 10:58 by another. The desk prints the ranges, because the sources do.

The day was invented quickly and argued about immediately. Within a year the silence had been improvised in Cape Town, proposed in print in London, carried through a South African statesman’s letter to the King’s private secretary, and proclaimed by George V for the whole Empire. The flower that came with it is a botanical point this report states plainly because it is widely gotten wrong: the Flanders poppy of remembrance is the corn poppy, Papaver rhoeas. The opium poppy is a different species, Papaver somniferum. The two are cousins, not the same plant, and the distinction is the whole of the symbol’s history—the corn poppy is the weed that colonized the churned chalk of the battlefields because its seeds can wait in disturbed soil for decades.

The date does not mean one thing. In the United States, November 11 began as Armistice Day, a day the 1938 statute said was “to be dedicated to the cause of world peace,” and became Veterans Day in 1954, honoring the living veterans of all wars. Kurt Vonnegut, born on the day in 1922 and a prisoner of war in Dresden in 1945, wrote the dissent that is still quoted: “Armistice Day was sacred. Veterans’ Day is not.” In France it is a public holiday for the dead of all France’s wars. In Poland it is Independence Day, marking a state reborn the same morning. In Germany it is nothing at all: the German national day of mourning, Volkstrauertag, falls this year on Sunday, November 15, and Germany’s first national day for veterans—created by the Bundestag in 2024, first observed June 15, 2025—is deliberately not a holiday and deliberately not in November. Russia left the war eight months before Compi&egrave;gne and keeps its First World War dead on August 1; its great day is May 9. And the question this report was asked—what is the World War II day?—has no single answer, because the second war ended in pieces: May 8 in most of Europe, May 9 in Moscow, August 15 in Britain, September 2 in the United States, September 3 in China and, since 2020, in Russia too.

1. The Eleventh Hour

The German delegation crossed the lines on the night of November 7–8, 1918, and was given seventy-two hours. It was headed by Matthias Erzberger, a Centre Party politician and Secretary of State, with Count Alfred von Oberndorff of the Foreign Ministry, Major-General Detlof von Winterfeldt for the army and Captain Ernst Vanselow for the navy. The convoy crossed the front in five cars on the evening of November 7 and was driven for some ten hours through the devastated north of France to Foch’s private train, standing in a siding in the Forest of Compi&egrave;gne at Rethondes. The carriage was dining car No. 2419D of the Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits. Marshal Ferdinand Foch, the Allied commander-in-chief, appeared in person only twice in the three days—at the opening, and at the signing. Admiral Rosslyn Wemyss, the British First Sea Lord, was the second Allied signatory. The coldness was policy. Erzberger asked for an immediate ceasefire while the terms were considered; in Joseph Persico’s widely quoted reconstruction he pleaded, “For God’s sake, Monsieur le Mar&eacute;chal, do not wait for those seventy-two hours. Stop the hostilities this very day.” Foch refused. The desk labels that sentence as reported dialogue from a secondary history; no stenographic transcript was located.

The terms were a dismantling. As printed in the signed text preserved in the United States State Department’s Foreign Relations volumes, the thirty-four clauses required: evacuation of Belgium, France, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine within fifteen days; Allied occupation of the left bank of the Rhine with bridgeheads thirty kilometres deep at Mainz, Koblenz and Cologne; surrender of 5,000 artillery pieces, 25,000 machine guns, 3,000 trench mortars and 1,700 aircraft; surrender of every submarine and internment of the High Seas Fleet’s modern units; delivery of 5,000 locomotives, 150,000 railway wagons and 5,000 motor lorries; renunciation of the Treaties of Brest-Litovsk and Bucharest; repatriation of Allied prisoners without reciprocity; and continuation of the naval blockade of Germany. While the delegation waited, the state that had sent it ceased to exist: on November 9 the Kaiser’s abdication was announced and a republic proclaimed in Berlin; on November 10 Wilhelm II crossed into the Netherlands, and Friedrich Ebert’s government instructed Erzberger to sign. The men who had arrived as envoys of an empire signed for a republic. Erzberger was vilified for it at home and assassinated by right-wing gunmen in 1921.

The signing time is a range, and the report prints it as one. The document itself is headed “signed at 5 o’clock A.M. (French time),” and the British government communiqu&eacute; Lloyd George read out said the same: “The armistice was signed at five o’clock this morning, and hostilities are to cease on all fronts at 11 a.m. to-day.” The Imperial War Museums give 05:00. The Australian War Memorial gives 05:10 in its main account and 05:15 in a second account by the historian Peter Hart; Persico also gives 05:10, “backed up officially to 5 a.m.” Compilatory sources run as late as 05:45. The honest statement is that the official time is 05:00, the best-supported time for pen on paper is about 05:10, and the full documented range is 05:00 to 05:45. Any account that prints one minute bare is claiming more than the record holds.

Three numbers are habitually confused, and they are different numbers. The seventy-two hours were Foch’s deadline to accept the terms. The six hours were Clause I’s interval between signing and effect: “Cessation of hostilities by land and in the air six hours after the signing of the armistice.” The thirty-six belongs to Clause XXXIV, which set the armistice’s duration at thirty-six days, renewable, and denounceable on forty-eight hours’ notice. There was no thirty-six-hour notice period. Foch’s implementing signal, preserved in the 2nd Australian Division’s copy and timed 06:35, read: “Hostilities will cease on the whole front on the 11th November French Time 11 Oclock. The Allied troops will not cross until further orders the line reached on that date at that time.” In Berlin, on Central European Time, the hour was noon. A story that Admiral Wemyss chose 11:00 for its poetry over a preferred 14:30 circulates in a community-contributed Imperial War Museums page; the desk found no better source for the motive and prints it as allegation only. The arithmetic needs no poetry: a 05:00 signature and a six-hour clause produce 11:00 on their own.

2. The Last Morning

The fighting continued because it was ordered to continue. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s official account states the rationale plainly: “Despite signing the Armistice in the early hours of the day, Allied commanders were still keen to keep the pressure on Imperial Germany militarily. Should fighting resume for any reason, the Allies decided they should be holding the best ground.” Foch’s standing instruction of November 9 was to maintain pressure until the ceasefire took effect. General Pershing’s notification to his commanders after the signing announced the hour; it did not order a halt before it. A divisional order quoted by Persico ran: “Hostilities will cease on the whole front at 11 hours today, French time. Until that hour, the operations previously ordered will be pressed with vigor. At 11 hours our line will halt in place, and no man will move one step forward or backward.” The morning’s attacks were therefore not, in the main, breakdowns of communication. They were the war, run to the last minute of its timetable.

The named operations carry their own records. On the Meuse, Major-General Charles P. Summerall ordered the 5th Division and attached Marines to force river crossings on the night of November 10–11, over pontoon bridges under machine-gun and shell fire; Persico counts more than 1,100 casualties in the final hours, a figure the desk prints as his count, no official V Corps tally having been located. At Stenay, Major-General William M. Wright carried out a planned attack with the 89th Division, which suffered 365 casualties including 61 dead; Wright’s own stated reason, from his diary as quoted by Persico, was that the division “had been in the line a considerable period without proper bathing facilities, and since it was realized that if the enemy were permitted to stay in Stenay, our troops would be deprived of the probable bathing facilities there.” Detractors alleged he wanted Stenay because it had been Crown Prince Rupprecht’s headquarters. Wright was succeeded in command the next day; whether the relief was punishment is alleged, not documented, and the desk does not print it as fact. At Mons, General Sir Arthur Currie received the news at 06:00 and Canadian troops completed the capture of the city that morning, at a cost commonly cited as 280 casualties to the Canadian Corps across November 10–11. Currie denied ever ordering an assault: “No order by me, verbal or otherwise, ordered an assault on Mons and Mons was never assaulted.” In the French sector, the 163rd Division attacked across the Meuse at Vrigne-Meuse under orders already in motion; figures of 75, 91 and “hundreds” for its November 11 dead all circulate, and the desk could not reconcile them.

The famous casualty figure is one historian’s estimate, and must be cited as one. Joseph E. Persico, in Eleventh Month, Eleventh Day, Eleventh Hour (2004), reconstructed from unit records an estimate of 10,944 casualties of all kinds on all sides on the Western Front on November 11, 1918, of whom 2,738 were killed—most of them in the six hours between signing and ceasefire, and at a rate he noted exceeded the war’s daily average. The Associated Press rounds the same estimate to 10,900. No official all-armies total exists. For the Commonwealth alone, the War Graves Commission’s records show 863 Commonwealth soldiers died on November 11, 1918—a figure narrower in every dimension: deaths only, one side’s forces only, counted by date of death, and including men who died that day of wounds received earlier. The two numbers measure different things and cannot be placed on the same axis. The American figures disputed before Congress illustrate the same problem from inside one army: the Army’s clerks supplied 268 Americans killed in action and 2,769 seriously wounded between midnight and 11:00; Persico’s reconstruction from the committee’s own papers puts American dead at at least 320 and total American casualties above 3,500, noting that the official return excluded divisions fighting under British and French command and conflicted with unit reports—one division officially reporting zero killed on a morning when one of its brigade commanders reported 191 killed and wounded. What is not in dispute, in any national account, is the order of magnitude of the morning: artillery and infantry attacks at operational tempo until 11:00, and the dead in the thousands in total casualties.

The named last deaths are documented, and their stopwatch order is not. Private George Edwin Ellison, 5th (Royal Irish) Lancers, a forty-year-old former Leeds miner who had fought from Mons in 1914, was killed on patrol outside Mons at 09:30 by the best-supported account, ninety minutes before the ceasefire. He lies in St Symphorien Military Cemetery, where his grave faces that of Private John Parr, the first British soldier killed in action on the Western Front, on August 21, 1914—a coincidence of a cemetery the German army created for the Mons dead of 1914, not a designed pairing. Private George Lawrence Price of the 28th Battalion, Canadian Infantry, was shot by a German sniper at Ville-sur-Haine as he stepped back into a street his patrol had just searched, and died at 10:58, the time his comrades’ 1968 plaque records and the War Graves Commission prints. The desk notes the conflict rather than hiding it: his battalion’s war diary gives 10:50 and a machine gun. Private Henry Nicholas Gunther of the 313th Infantry, a Baltimore bank clerk and the son of German immigrants, demoted from sergeant after a censored letter home, charged a German machine-gun roadblock near Chaumont-devant-Damvillers whose gunners—who knew the armistice was minutes away—tried to wave him off; he fired, they returned a short burst, and he died instantly. Pershing’s Order of the Day on November 12 named him the last American killed in the war. The National Archives gives his death at 10:59 in its burial-card article and at 10:58, quoting a war diary, in its centenary article; on the second timing Gunther and Price are simultaneous. The desk prints Gunther as generally recognised as the last, and the superlative as a convention of the record, not a stopwatch certainty. The last French soldier killed, Augustin Tr&eacute;buchon of the 415th Infantry Regiment, a shepherd and regimental runner, died at Vrigne-Meuse carrying a message; accounts put his death between 10:45 and 10:55. A figure of 09:15 attached to Tr&eacute;buchon in some retellings was found in no source the desk consulted and is not printed. French graves of November 11 dead in the Vrigne-Meuse sector bear the date November 10; the graves are documented, and an official order to backdate—and the motive for one, shame or clerical practice—remains alleged in both directions. No last German death of the morning is reliably documented by name and time.

Congress asked, and then Congress withdrew the question. On November 5, 1919, Pershing told the House Committee on Military Affairs that “the mere discussion of an armistice would not be sufficient grounds for any judicious commander to relax his military activities.” Representative Alvan Fuller forwarded a constituent letter from a former artillery operations officer lamenting “the little crosses over the graves of the colored lads who died a useless death on that November morning” and asked for “a real frank, full answer to the question as to whether American lives were needlessly wasted.” Pershing replied that he had followed Foch’s November 9 orders and had no knowledge of the signing before 06:00; Persico calls that claim disingenuous, and the desk prints both characterisations attributed. A separate body, Subcommittee 3 of the House Select Committee on Expenditures in the War Department, chaired by Royal C. Johnson—himself a decorated veteran of Gunther’s own regiment—investigated the Armistice Day losses through the winter. By the end of January 1920 Johnson’s draft concluded that “needless slaughter” had occurred, and the full committee initially adopted it. Daniel Flood filed a minority report charging defamation of the commanders. On March 3, 1920, under pressure not to hold up the committee’s report, Johnson struck every imputation that American lives had been needlessly sacrificed. The verified outcome of the only official inquiry into the last morning is therefore: hearings held, a verdict drafted and adopted, the verdict withdrawn, and no commander sanctioned.

3. The War’s Other Endings

November 11 is a Western Front date because the war ended in pieces. Russia left first: the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed March 3, 1918, took the new Bolshevik state out of the war eight months before Compi&egrave;gne, at the price of vast western territories. Bulgaria signed the Armistice of Salonica on September 29, 1918. The Ottoman Empire signed at Mudros on October 30. Austria-Hungary signed at Villa Giusti on November 3, effective at 15:00 on November 4—which is why Italy keeps November 4, not November 11. In East Africa, German forces under Lettow-Vorbeck, who had heard nothing, fought on until November 25. An armistice is a suspension of fighting, not a peace: the Compi&egrave;gne instrument ran thirty-six days at a time and was renewed while the blockade continued. The peace with Germany, the Treaty of Versailles, was signed June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors. The United States, whose Senate refused Versailles, ended its own war separately—by the Knox–Porter joint resolution of July 2, 1921, and the Treaty of Berlin of August 25, 1921. The ratifications of that treaty were exchanged on November 11, 1921, the day the American Unknown Soldier was buried at Arlington. The Western Front’s date became the world’s date by usage, not by fact; Section 12 of this report takes up the countries for whom the date means something else entirely.

4. The Invention of Remembrance

The first anniversary was proclaimed, not legislated. On November 11, 1919, President Woodrow Wilson issued an “Address to Fellow-Countrymen”—not a numbered proclamation, and it created no holiday—recalling that a year earlier “our enemies laid down their arms” and that the achievement had been bought at a cost the country was still counting. The federal holiday came nineteen years later (Section 7). In London, George V’s message appeared in The Times of November 7, 1919—the Australian War Memorial dates the Commonwealth message November 6; both are printed here because both stand in the record—asking that at the eleventh hour there be, throughout the Empire, a complete suspension of ordinary business and a silence of two minutes. The London observance of 1919 was improvised around a monument that did not yet exist in permanent form.

The silence has three documented parents, and the Imperial War Museums credit none of them. The earliest documented practice is Cape Town’s. After news of the German spring offensive reached South Africa, the mayor, Sir Harry Hands—whose own son had been killed in April 1918—instituted a midday pause: a notice in the Cape Times of May 13, 1918 announced three minutes from May 14, one for the fallen, one for prayer for those still fighting, one for the living; within days it was cut to two minutes, and it ran daily, signalled by a noon gun and maroons, with trams stopping and men baring their heads. The transmission to London is documented: Sir Percy FitzPatrick, the South African author and statesman, wrote to Lord Stamfordham, the King’s private secretary, proposing that the Cape Town practice be taken up Empire-wide on the anniversary; the letter survives in the Royal Archives. The third claimant, the Australian journalist Edward Honey, is documented only as a publication: an article in the London Evening News of May 8, 1919 proposed a silence of five minutes. The Imperial War Museums’ account names no originator. The desk’s statement is the one the evidence supports: the practice is documented first in Cape Town, the proposal’s route to the King is documented in FitzPatrick’s letter, Honey proposed a longer silence in print independently, and the two minutes the world kept are Cape Town’s length, not Honey’s.

The Cenotaph was a temporary stage prop that the public refused to give up. Edwin Lutyens designed a wood-and-plaster cenotaph—the word means an empty tomb—for the Peace Day parade of July 19, 1919. Crowds left flowers and wreaths at its base in such volume that it was rebuilt in Portland stone on the same Whitehall site and unveiled by George V at 11:00 on November 11, 1920, as part of the funeral procession of the Unknown Warrior. The British Unknown Warrior himself had been chosen at Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise—not Saint-Omer, as many accounts print—where four bodies exhumed from four battlefields were laid out and one was selected, blind, by a brigadier; he was buried in Westminster Abbey on November 11, 1920. A correction the desk makes because the error is common: the Unknown Warrior received no Victoria Cross. The Cross enters the story twice around him—a guard of honour of one hundred Victoria Cross holders stood over his grave, and he was awarded the American Medal of Honor, presented by General Pershing on October 17, 1921. The reciprocal award closed the circle on November 11, 1921, when Admiral Beatty presented the Victoria Cross to the American Unknown Soldier at his burial in Arlington.

France and America built the same idea on different days. The French Unknown Soldier was presented beneath the Arc de Triomphe on November 11, 1920, but buried there on January 28, 1921; he had been chosen the day before the presentation at Verdun by a young soldier, Auguste Thin, who laid a bouquet on one of eight coffins. The eternal flame at the tomb was first lit by the Minister of War, Andr&eacute; Maginot, on November 11, 1923, and has been rekindled daily at 18:30 ever since, including through the Occupation. France’s own November 11, 1919 had been a single discreet ceremony in a chapel of the Invalides; the French public holiday dates from the law of October 24, 1922. At Arlington on November 11, 1921, the American Unknown was buried with full honours; Woodrow Wilson, broken in health, rode in the Washington procession—whether he reached the amphitheatre itself is disputed in the sources, and the desk leaves it open.

5. The Flower

First, the plant, because the day’s symbol is persistently misdescribed, including in the commissioning conversation for this report, as “the flower from the opium plant.” It is not. The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, identifies the remembrance poppy as Papaver rhoeas, the corn poppy—also called the field poppy, Flanders poppy and red poppy—a common annual weed of cornfields and disturbed ground across Europe. The opium poppy is Papaver somniferum, a separate species, the plant of the opium trade and the source plant of morphine and codeine. The two are congeners within the genus Papaver; they are not the same species, and the red flower on a November lapel is the corn poppy. The desk states the correction carefully and stops where the botany stops: the corn poppy is not a drug crop and is not the opium plant, but it is a member of a chemically active genus, and this report makes no unqualified claim that the plant contains no alkaloids of any kind—a pharmacopoeial entry located in research asserts the presence of thebaine-type compounds, and the qualified statement is the safe one. What made rhoeas the flower of the battlefields is its seed. Kew documents that corn poppy seeds can lie dormant in soil for eighty years or more and germinate when the ground is disturbed; Veterans Affairs Canada adds the chemistry of the trenches—the chalk and lime of shell-torn, rubble-strewn ground suited the plant exactly. The poppies of 1915 were not planted. They were what the ploughed graveyard of the Western Front grew by itself.

The poem came first, and it was published anonymously. Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae, a Canadian physician serving with the Canadian Field Artillery, wrote “In Flanders Fields” at Ypres in the days after the death of his friend Lieutenant Alexis Helmer, killed on May 2, 1915; the poem was composed, by the standard account, on or about May 3, among graves already marked with wooden crosses and already growing poppies. Punch published it, unsigned, on December 8, 1915: “In Flanders fields the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row.” The poem’s last verse is an instruction—“Take up our quarrel with the foe: / To you from failing hands we throw / The Torch; be yours to hold it high”—and the organisations that took the poppy up understood themselves as answering it. McCrae did not live to see the symbol: he died of pneumonia in January 1918.

Two women carried the flower from the poem to the lapel. Moina Michael, an American professor serving with the YMCA in New York, read the poem in November 1918 and answered it with a poem of her own, “We Shall Keep the Faith,” and a vow to wear a red poppy; she is the documented origin of the poppy as an emblem worn. Anna Gu&eacute;rin, a Frenchwoman who had seen the poem’s effect in America, is the documented origin of the poppy as an article sold for veterans: she organised the manufacture of artificial poppies in France—made, in the first instance, by war widows and orphans—and carried the Poppy Day idea to Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand in person in 1920–21. The veterans’ organisations adopted in sequence: the American Legion named the poppy its official flower on September 27, 1920, at its Cleveland convention; Canada’s Great War Veterans’ Association adopted it in July 1921—the Legion’s poppy history and Veterans Affairs Canada differ by a day, July 5 or July 6, and the desk prints the month—and held its first Poppy Day on November 11, 1921; and in London, Major George Howson and the Royal British Legion, founded that May, adopted Gu&eacute;rin’s proposal for the first Poppy Appeal of November 11, 1921, which raised &pound;106,000. The desk prints that figure alone; modern equivalents offered by sources range so widely—&pound;1.3 million to &pound;30 million in the material consulted—that any one of them would be a false precision.

The making of the poppies is part of the symbol, and its history is specific. From the start, the British appeal’s poppies were to be made by disabled ex-servicemen. The Poppy Factory was founded on June 5, 1922—on the Old Kent Road in London, not in Richmond, whither it moved in 1926—employing disabled veterans to make the wreaths and poppies. The present-day division of labour, verified for this report, is that the Richmond factory makes the wreaths and ceremonial work, while the bulk of the lapel poppies are machine-made at Aylesford in Kent. In 2023 the Legion replaced the plastic poppy with a plastic-free, 100-per-cent paper poppy, launched on October 26, 2023. The money remains large: the Legion’s Annual Report records &pound;41.9 million for the 2023 appeal, an announced &pound;51.4 million for the 2024 appeal, and &pound;56.6 million reported for the 2025 appeal; the desk prints the three figures with their years and measures attached, because the appeal’s totals are reported on different bases in different documents and an unattributed single figure would mislead. In Scotland the poppy is its own: four petals and no leaf, made at Lady Haig’s Poppy Factory in Edinburgh, under Poppyscotland, which merged into the Legion in 2011 while remaining a distinct Scottish charity. In New Zealand the first Poppy Day, in 1922, fell not in November at all but on Anzac Day, April 24, because the shipment of French-made poppies arrived late—a logistics accident that anticipated the southern pattern described in Section 9. In the United States the flower’s anchor is the other war-dead day: the American Legion’s Poppy Day and the Veterans of Foreign Wars’ Buddy Poppy—distributed nationwide from before Memorial Day 1922, its trademark registered in February 1924, made historically by disabled veterans in hospitals—belong to Memorial Day in May, though both organisations also distribute poppies on Veterans Day. No record of trademark litigation over the Buddy Poppy was found in this research, and none is claimed.

6. The Other Flowers and the Quarrels

France’s flower is blue, and older as an organised symbol than the British poppy appeal. The bleuet—the cornflower—was first made at Les Invalides in 1916, in workshops organised by Suzanne Lenhardt, the hospital’s head nurse and a war widow (official French sources divide on the spelling, Leenhardt or Lenhardt; the desk uses the form in the charity’s own history), and Charlotte Malleterre, where wounded soldiers made tissue cornflowers for sale for their own benefit. The official chronology of the &OElig;uvre nationale du Bleuet de France runs: association in 1934, a nationwide collection in 1935, a second collection day on May 8 added in 1957, and absorption into the national veterans’ office, ONACVG, in 1991. The blue is officially explained three ways at once: the cornflowers that grew, like the poppies, in the battlefield mud; the blue of the tricolour; and the bleu horizon, the blue-grey uniform of the young conscripts, the bleus, who arrived at the front as the cornflowers flowered. Two flowers, one flora: the Allies’ symbols were both, in origin, the weeds of the same fields, sorted by nation.

Serbia’s flower is a resurrection plant, chosen by politicians in 2012. Serbia made Armistice Day a state holiday in 2012, and its emblem pairs Natalie’s ramonda, Ramonda nathaliae, with the green-and-black ribbon of the Albanian Commemorative Medal. The botany is genuinely remarkable and documented in the botanical literature: the ramonda is a resurrection plant, able to survive near-complete desiccation and revive when watered, and it was adopted as a figure for Serbia’s own recovery after 1918—a country that lost, on the attributed range the desk found, between 1.1 and 1.3 million people, the sources in conflict on the toll of the state that suffered proportionally among the worst of the war.
